docs.title: Tileverse
docs.text: Tileverse is a set of Java libraries for cloud-native geospatial applications. Each library solves one problem: object storage, tile archives, vector tile encoding, or tile grids. Use the ones you need, alone or together.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
Library Artifact Use it to Storage tileverse-storage-all List, read, write and presign objects on local disks, HTTP, S3, Azure and GCS through one API, and read byte ranges of single files. PMTiles tileverse-pmtiles Read PMTiles archives, as tile bytes or as decoded vector and raster tiles. Versatiles tileverse-versatiles Read VersaTiles containers, as tile bytes or as decoded vector and raster tiles. Vector Tiles tileverse-vectortiles Encode and decode Mapbox Vector Tiles with JTS geometries. Tile Matrix Set tileverse-tilematrixset Map coordinates to tiles with the OGC Tile Matrix Set model. Tile Store tileverse-tilestore Read tiles through one API, whatever the archive format.

Getting Started shows how to add them to a project.

docs.title: How they fit together
docs.text:
The archive readers build on the other libraries. Storage, Vector Tiles and Tile Matrix Set are independent of each other:

  • Building a GeoParquet datastore that lists and reads partitioned files in S3, Azure or GCS? Use Storage.
  • Reading Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs with byte-range requests? Use the RangeReader API of Storage.
  • Building a tile server from PostGIS? Use Vector Tiles and Tile Matrix Set.
  • Need a standard grid definition? Use Tile Matrix Set.

docs.title: AI policy
docs.text: Contributors and users may use AI tools for project work. To keep the code sound, the project secure and the community healthy, contributions follow the rules below.

docs.title: Code and documentation
docs.text:
These rules hold for each contribution, however it was produced:

  1. Responsibility. The contributor answers for the contribution: its correctness, design, copyright, license and fit for the project.
  2. Understanding. The contributor understands the design, the implementation and the effects of the contribution. Do not submit a contribution if you cannot explain it.
  3. Correctness. The contributor checks that the contribution is correct, complete, and consistent with the architecture and conventions of the project. AI tools make mistakes, and catching them is the job of the contributor.
  4. Feasibility. A contribution stays within what the contributor could have produced alone, with reasonable research and discussion. AI tools speed the work up. They do not replace the expertise required by the work.
  5. Maintainability. The contributor and the other project members must be able to maintain the contribution over time. Needless complexity and length, in code or in documentation, are a lasting cost.

docs.title: Security reports
docs.text: AI tools may help find and write up a security report. The reporter checks that the problem is real and reproducible before sending it. A report includes a working reproduction (code, configuration or a request) against a released version or main, not only a plausible description. If a report turns out to be invented or impossible to verify, it is closed without further discussion.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
These guidelines apply to issues, pull requests and their comments. Keep messages short and to the point: few readers have time for long prose.

  • State your point in the first sentence. That is where the reader decides whether to read on.
  • Keep a message to about one screen. If it needs more, add a final section with the details. A reader must be able to skip it without missing the main points.
  • One topic per message.
  • Many participants are not native English speakers. Use simple, common words.
  • Avoid heavy AI-style formatting (headings, bold key terms, nested bullets), even in short messages. If a message reads like AI slop, readers discount it before reading its content.

In pull requests:

  • Comment on code inline, on the line concerned.
  • Use a top-level comment for what does not belong to a line: the overall approach, missing tests, scope.
  • Link to code or documentation outside the pull request when you refer to it.

In issues:

  • The title names the observed symptom, not your guess at its cause.
  • The description gives the expected and the actual behavior. Use a numbered list for the steps only when they happen in order.
  • Add small data samples, configuration or requests to reproduce the problem on someone else's machine.

Adapted from the GeoServer AI policy.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Tileverse is a set of loosely coupled libraries. Each module works on its own, for one domain: I/O, tile grids, or tile encodings.

docs.title: System context
docs.text: The Tileverse system sits between consumer applications and five external storage families: local FS, HTTP, S3-compatible object stores, Azure and GCS.

docs.title: Container view
docs.text:
The library modules, their dependencies on each other, and their dependencies on the external storage systems. tileverse-pmtiles and tileverse-versatiles depend on every other Tileverse module; tileverse-tilestore brings the format-agnostic TileStore<T> abstraction; the four storage containers (-core, -s3, -azure, -gcs) compose under -all for callers that want every backend at once.

Per-module C4 component views are embedded in each library's section:

  • Storage core internals
  • PMTiles internals
  • Versatiles internals
  • Vector Tiles internals
  • Tile Matrix Set internals
  • Tile Stores internals

All C4 diagrams are generated from docs/structurizr/workspace.dsl and docs/structurizr/dynamic-views.dsl via docs/build.sh (Docker required). Edit the DSL and rerun the build to regenerate.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• I/O stays separate from formats. A format library, such as a GeoTIFF reader, should not implement its own S3 client. Storage provides the container API, and its RangeReader the byte-range reads of single files.
  • Grid math needs no GIS library. tileverse-tilematrixset computes tile coordinates and bounding boxes with no GIS or I/O library; it depends on Jackson for its JSON encoding. A tile server can use it whatever its data source.
  • Codecs do no I/O. tileverse-vectortiles converts between the protobuf encoding and JTS geometries.
  • Archive readers compose the rest. tileverse-pmtiles and tileverse-versatiles read through a RangeReader, use the tile matrix set for the grid, and decode tiles with the vector tile codec or javax.imageio.

docs.title: Reading a tile
docs.text:
When a PMTilesReader reads the tile (z, x, y):

  1. It computes the tile id of the tile along the Hilbert curve.
  2. It looks the id up in the directories. A directory missing from its cache costs one range request.
  3. It reads the tile body with one range request, and removes the tile compression of the archive.
  4. A tile store decodes the bytes: PMTilesVectorTileStore with VectorTileCodec, and PMTilesRasterTileStore with javax.imageio.ImageIO. The decoder reads from a stream over a pooled buffer holding the tile bytes.

PMTilesReader keeps parsed directories in its own cache, and block-aligns its reads of the header, the directories and the metadata. Tile bytes are cached only when the reader passed to PMTilesReader is a CachingRangeReader.

docs.title: Extension points
docs.text:
• Implement StorageProvider, registered through ServiceLoader, to add a storage backend: for example an internal content-addressed store, a store with its own URI scheme, or a test harness. Native protocols like OpenStack Swift, Azure Files (SMB), or HDFS through WebHDFS are out of scope; see Why tileverse-storage?.
  • Subclass AbstractTileStore<T> to expose a different archive format under the same TileStore<T> contract, as tileverse-versatiles does for VersaTiles containers. MBTiles would fit the same way.
  • Implement TileMatrixSet to support non-Earth or custom grids while reusing the rest of the stack unchanged.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Java 17 or later, to build and to run. CI also builds on Java 21 and 25.
  • Maven 3.9 or later. The repository includes the Maven wrapper, ./mvnw.
  • Docker, for the integration tests.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
The Makefile wraps the common tasks:

make            # install the modules into the local Maven repository, then run the tests
make compile    # compile only
make test       # run the tests
make format     # format the Java sources and sort the POMs
make lint       # check the formatting and the license headers, as CI does
make clean      # remove the build output

With Maven directly:

./mvnw clean package                              # build and test
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests                  # build without the tests
./mvnw clean package -pl :tileverse-pmtiles -am   # one module and the modules it needs

Select modules by artifact id (-pl :artifactId), and add -am to also build the modules they depend on.

Each Maven build formats the Java sources with Spotless, in the Palantir style, and sorts the POMs with SortPOM. -Dqa switches both to check mode, as in CI. -Dcoverage adds JaCoCo and the aggregate coverage report.

Spotless also adds the license header from license_header.txt to new Java files, and -Dqa fails on a file without it. Spotless skips package-info.java files: copy the header into them by hand.

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Unit tests (*Test.java) use JUnit 5 and Mockito. Integration tests (*IT.java) run against real services in Docker containers, through Testcontainers.

./mvnw test                                   # unit tests, or make test-unit
./mvnw verify                                 # unit and integration tests, or make test-it
./mvnw verify -pl :tileverse-storage-s3 -am   # the tests of one module

The integration tests use these images:

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: Contributions are welcome. If you use AI tools, read the AI policy first.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and clone it.
  2. Create a branch, for example feat/my-feature or fix/my-bug.
  3. Make the change, with unit tests for new logic. Changes to the cloud backends also need integration tests.
  4. Build with ./mvnw verify. The build formats the code.
  5. Open a pull request against main.

The pull request template lists what a pull request needs before the merge:

  • New unit tests cover the change.
  • The documentation is updated, if users can see the change.
  • A GitHub issue describes the change, unless users see no difference.
  • A bug fix or a small feature is a single commit, and each commit has a single goal.

The pull request is merged when the build checks are green, a maintainer has reviewed it, and the checklist is complete.

docs.title: Coding standards
docs.text:
• Target Java 17. The build runs on Java 17 and later.
  • Follow the Palantir Java Format. The build applies it.
  • Start each Java file with the license header from license_header.txt. The build adds it, except to package-info.java files.
  • Document the public API with javadoc.
  • Return Optional<T> for a value that may be missing. Avoid returning null.

  • fix: handle EOF correctly in range reader
  • docs: update usage examples
  • chore: bump dependencies

docs.title: PMTiles
docs.text:
This module reads PMTiles version 3 archives, a single-file format for map tiles. The reader fetches only the bytes it needs, with range requests. This suits archives served from object storage or HTTP.

The module reads archives and does not write them. To create an archive, use a tool such as pmtiles or Tippecanoe.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
A PMTiles archive has four parts:

  1. Header: 127 bytes at the start of the file. It records the tile type, the compression of the tiles and of the directories, the zoom range, the bounds, and the location of the other parts.
  2. Directories: the index of the tiles. A root directory sits near the start of the file, and large archives add leaf directories.
  3. Metadata: a JSON document.
  4. Tile data: the tile bodies.

To read a tile, the reader turns its position into a tile id along a Hilbert curve, finds the id in the directories, and reads the tile body. Parsed directories stay in a cache.

Tiles are addressed with the XYZ scheme: zoom level, column from west to east, and row from north to south. The header records the tile type: MVT, PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, MLT, or unknown. The reader returns the tiles of any type, after removing the tile compression of the archive. The tile stores decode MVT tiles to VectorTile objects, and PNG, JPEG, WebP and AVIF tiles to RenderedImage objects.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.tileverse.pmtiles</groupId>
    <artifactId>tileverse-pmtiles</artifactId>
</dependency>

The version comes from tileverse-bom, as described in Getting Started. Local files and HTTP work out of the box. S3, Azure and GCS URIs need tileverse-storage-all, or the matching tileverse-storage-s3, tileverse-storage-azure or tileverse-storage-gcs module, next to tileverse-pmtiles.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.PMTilesHeader;
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.PMTilesReader;
import io.tileverse.tiling.pyramid.TileIndex;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Optional;

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(Path.of("data/map.pmtiles").toUri())) {
    PMTilesHeader header = reader.getHeader();
    System.out.println("Tile type: " + header.tileMimeType());
    System.out.println("Zoom levels: " + header.minZoom() + " to " + header.maxZoom());

    // The buffer is ready to read, do not flip it
    Optional<ByteBuffer> tile = reader.getTile(TileIndex.zxy(0, 0, 0));
}

PMTilesReader.open(URI) accepts the URIs supported by tileverse-storage, such as s3://bucket/map.pmtiles or https://example.com/map.pmtiles.

docs.title: Component view
docs.text: PMTilesReader is the low-level type. It reads the header, finds a tile in the directories through the HilbertCurve, and returns the tile bytes. It can also stream them through an IOFunction supplied by the caller. PMTilesVectorTileStore and PMTilesRasterTileStore wrap a PMTilesReader and decode tiles to VectorTile and RenderedImage objects.

docs.title: Reading PMTiles archives
docs.text: This guide shows how to open a PMTiles archive, read its tiles, and decode them.

docs.title: Open an archive
docs.text:
PMTilesReader.open opens the Storage of the parent location and gets a RangeReader for the file. Closing the PMTilesReader closes both. The call accepts a URI with a scheme supported by tileverse-storage. The cloud schemes need their storage module, as described in Installation.

import io.tileverse.pmtiles.PMTilesReader;
import java.net.URI;
import java.nio.file.Path;

// Local file
PMTilesReader fileReader = PMTilesReader.open(Path.of("map.pmtiles").toUri());

// HTTP
PMTilesReader httpReader = PMTilesReader.open(URI.create("https://example.com/map.pmtiles"));

// S3, Azure, and GCS use the same call
PMTilesReader s3Reader = PMTilesReader.open(URI.create("s3://bucket/map.pmtiles"));

To configure the storage backend, for example its region, credentials, or endpoint, pass a StorageConfig. The storage configuration guide and the authentication guide list the parameters.

import io.tileverse.storage.StorageConfig;

StorageConfig config = new StorageConfig(URI.create("s3://bucket/map.pmtiles"))
        .setParameter("storage.s3.region", "us-west-2");

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(config)) {
    // ...
}

To read through a RangeReader opened by your own code, pass it to the constructor. The PMTilesReader takes ownership of the RangeReader and closes it in close(). The following example caches the ranges read from S3 in memory:

import io.tileverse.storage.RangeReader;
import io.tileverse.storage.Storage;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageFactory;
import io.tileverse.storage.cache.CachingRangeReader;

try (Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(URI.create("s3://bucket/"));
        PMTilesReader reader = new PMTilesReader(CachingRangeReader.of(storage.openRangeReader("map.pmtiles")))) {
    // ...
}

Opening an archive reads its header and its metadata. An InvalidHeaderException means the file is not a PMTiles version 3 archive.

docs.title: Read the header and metadata
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.jackson.databind.pmtiles.v3.PMTilesMetadata;
import io.tileverse.jackson.databind.tilejson.v3.VectorLayer;
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.PMTilesHeader;
import java.util.List;

PMTilesHeader header = reader.getHeader();
byte tileType = header.tileType();          // PMTilesHeader.TILETYPE_MVT, TILETYPE_PNG, ...
String mimeType = header.tileMimeType();    // "application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile", "image/webp", ...
boolean raster = header.isRasterTileType();
int minZoom = header.minZoom();
int maxZoom = header.maxZoom();

// The bounds are in degrees, stored multiplied by 10,000,000
double minLon = header.minLonE7() / 10_000_000.0;
double minLat = header.minLatE7() / 10_000_000.0;
double maxLon = header.maxLonE7() / 10_000_000.0;
double maxLat = header.maxLatE7() / 10_000_000.0;

PMTilesMetadata metadata = reader.getMetadata();
String name = metadata.name();
List<VectorLayer> layers = metadata.vectorLayers();

String json = reader.getMetadataAsString();  // the metadata document, decompressed

docs.title: Read tiles
docs.text:
getTile returns the bytes of a tile after removing the tile compression of the archive, or an empty Optional when the archive has no tile at that position. The buffer is ready to read. Do not flip it.

import io.tileverse.tiling.pyramid.TileIndex;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.util.Optional;

Optional<ByteBuffer> tile = reader.getTile(TileIndex.zxy(10, 885, 412));

getTile(long) takes the PMTiles tile id instead, and reader.getTileId(tileIndex) converts a TileIndex to it.

To decode a tile as it is read, pass a function to getTile with the tile id. The function receives the tile bytes as an InputStream, and getTile returns its result. This overload avoids a copy of the tile into a ByteBuffer:

import io.tileverse.io.IOFunction;
import java.io.InputStream;

IOFunction<InputStream, byte[]> toBytes = InputStream::readAllBytes;
Optional<byte[]> bytes = reader.getTile(reader.getTileId(TileIndex.zxy(10, 885, 412)), toBytes);

PMTilesReader is thread-safe. Several threads can read tiles from one reader at the same time:

IntStream.rangeClosed(880, 890).parallel().forEach(x ->
        IntStream.rangeClosed(410, 420).forEach(y -> {
            try {
                reader.getTile(TileIndex.zxy(10, x, y)).ifPresent(tile -> process(x, y, tile));
            } catch (IOException e) {
                throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
            }
        }));

docs.title: Decode tiles with a tile store
docs.text:
The tile stores wrap a PMTilesReader and implement the TileStore<T> API described in the Tile Stores Reference. They decode tiles to the payload type of the store:

Tile type Store Payload MVT PMTilesVectorTileStore io.tileverse.vectortile.model.VectorTile PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF PMTilesRasterTileStore java.awt.image.RenderedImage

A store checks the tile type of the archive when it is created. It throws UnsupportedTileTypeException when the archive holds another type. To pick the store from the archive:

import io.tileverse.tiling.store.TileStore;

TileStore<?> store = reader.getHeader().isRasterTileType()
        ? new PMTilesRasterTileStore(reader)
        : new PMTilesVectorTileStore(reader);

The stores borrow the reader. Close the reader when you are done; a store holds no other resources.

docs.title: Read vector tiles
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.store.PMTilesVectorTileStore;
import io.tileverse.tiling.store.TileData;
import io.tileverse.vectortile.model.VectorTile;

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(uri)) {
    PMTilesVectorTileStore store = new PMTilesVectorTileStore(reader);

    Optional<TileData<VectorTile>> data = store.findTile(TileIndex.zxy(10, 885, 412));
    data.ifPresent(td -> {
        VectorTile vectorTile = td.data();
        // walk layers and features...
    });
}

store.getVectorLayersMetadata() returns the vector_layers of the archive metadata.

docs.title: Read raster tiles
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.store.PMTilesRasterTileStore;
import java.awt.image.RenderedImage;

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(uri)) {
    PMTilesRasterTileStore store = new PMTilesRasterTileStore(reader);

    System.out.println("MIME type: " + store.mimeType());  // "image/webp", "image/png", ...

    Optional<TileData<RenderedImage>> data = store.findTile(TileIndex.zxy(10, 885, 412));
}

PNG and JPEG decoders come with the JDK, and tileverse-pmtiles brings a WebP decoder for javax.imageio. AVIF needs an ImageIO plugin of your own.

loadTile reports I/O errors as UncheckedIOException, because the TileStore API declares no checked exceptions.

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
Keep a reader open and reuse it: opening an archive reads its header and its metadata.

For a remote archive, wrap the RangeReader in a CachingRangeReader, as shown in Open an archive. The reader aligns its reads of the header, the directories and the metadata to blocks, and the cache keeps those blocks. Tile reads stay exact. The storage configuration guide describes the size of the cache.

A reader also keeps parsed directories in a cache, and the vector store caches decoded tiles. Both caches belong to CacheManager.getDefault() unless you set another CacheManager:

import io.tileverse.cache.CacheManager;

CacheManager cacheManager = CacheManager.newInstance();
reader.cacheManager(cacheManager);

// For the vector store, this sets the cache manager of the store and of its reader
PMTilesVectorTileStore store = new PMTilesVectorTileStore(reader).cacheManager(cacheManager);

docs.title: Handle errors
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.pmtiles.InvalidHeaderException;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageException;
import java.io.IOException;

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(uri)) {
    Optional<ByteBuffer> tile = reader.getTile(TileIndex.zxy(zoom, x, y));
} catch (InvalidHeaderException e) {
    // Not a PMTiles archive, or a version this reader does not support
} catch (StorageException e) {
    // The storage failed; NotFoundException when the file is missing
} catch (IOException e) {
    // Unreadable directories, metadata or tile compression
}

InvalidHeaderException and StorageException (in io.tileverse.storage) are unchecked.

docs.title: Tile Stores Reference
docs.text:
The *TileStore classes wrap a PMTilesReader and expose a uniform, format-agnostic API parameterized on the decoded payload type. The store abstractions live in the tileverse-tilestore module, and the PMTiles stores live in tileverse-pmtiles. tileverse-tilestore is pulled in transitively when you depend on tileverse-pmtiles; no separate dependency is needed.

This page is the API reference. For task-oriented walkthroughs see Reading PMTiles.

docs.title: Component view
docs.text: TileStore<T> is the format-agnostic top-level interface; AbstractTileStore<T> owns the TileMatrixSet. VectorTileStore and RasterTileStore are payload-specific abstract bases that PMTiles (and any future archive format) implements. The TileJSON v3 Model records expose per-layer metadata advertised by vector archives.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text: Package Type Purpose io.tileverse.tiling.store TileStore<T> Top-level interface: query by extent, by zoom, or one tile at a time. io.tileverse.tiling.store AbstractTileStore<T> Base class that owns the TileMatrixSet. io.tileverse.tiling.store TileData<T> Record pairing a Tile (spatial metadata) with its decoded payload. io.tileverse.vectortile.store VectorTileStore Abstract base for stores whose payload is a decoded VectorTile. io.tileverse.vectortile.store VectorTilesQuery Feature query for VectorTileStore.getFeatures: layers, zoom or resolution, extent, filter. io.tileverse.rastertile.store RasterTileStore Abstract base for stores whose payload is a decoded RenderedImage. io.tileverse.pmtiles.store PMTilesVectorTileStore PMTiles archive whose tileType == TILETYPE_MVT. io.tileverse.pmtiles.store PMTilesRasterTileStore PMTiles archive whose tileType == TILETYPE_{PNG,JPEG,WEBP,AVIF}. io.tileverse.jackson.databind.tilejson.v3 TileJSON, VectorLayer, TilesetType TileJSON 3.0.0 model exposed by VectorTileStore.getVectorLayersMetadata() and produced by serializers.

docs.title: TileStore<T>
docs.text:
public interface TileStore<T> {
    enum Strategy { SPEED, QUALITY }

    TileMatrixSet matrixSet();
    Optional<TileData<T>> loadTile(Tile tile);
    default Optional<TileData<T>> findTile(TileIndex tileIndex);

    default Stream<TileData<T>> findTiles(List<BoundingBox2D> extents, int zoomLevel);
    default Stream<TileData<T>> findTiles(List<BoundingBox2D> extents, double resolution, Strategy strategy);
    default Optional<TileMatrix> tileMatrix(List<BoundingBox2D> extents, int zoomLevel);
    default int findBestZoomLevel(double resolution, Strategy strategy);
    default int findBestZoomLevel(double resolution, Strategy strategy, int minZoomLevel, int maxZoomLevel);
}
  • matrixSet() returns the store's grid model. For PMTiles this is WebMercatorQuad, or WebMercatorQuadx2 for a raster archive of 512 px tiles, limited to the archive's zoom range and bounds: findTile returns empty for a tile outside them, and getTileMatrix(z) throws for a zoom outside the range.
  • loadTile(Tile) is the single primitive every subclass implements. Default methods compose it.
  • findTile(TileIndex) resolves the index through the matrix set and loads that tile.
  • findTiles resolves a list of extents to the intersecting tile range and streams decoded payloads.
  • Strategy controls zoom selection when a target resolution falls between matrix levels. SPEED rounds to the coarser zoom (fewer reads), QUALITY rounds to the finer zoom (more detail).

docs.title: TileData<T>
docs.text:
public record TileData<T>(Tile tile, T data) {}

Tile holds spatial metadata: its TileIndex, its extent in CRS units, its size in pixels, its resolution and the CRS id. data is the decoded payload of type T. Useful when a consumer needs the extent to position the tile in a mosaic without re-deriving it.

docs.title: VectorTileStore
docs.text:
public abstract class VectorTileStore extends AbstractTileStore<VectorTile> {
    public abstract List<VectorLayer> getVectorLayersMetadata();
    public Optional<VectorLayer> getLayerMetadata(String layerId);
    public abstract BoundingBox2D getExtent();
    public Stream<Feature> getFeatures(VectorTilesQuery query);
}
  • getVectorLayersMetadata() returns the TileJSON 3.0.0 vector_layers array advertised by the archive (layer id, field types, zoom range).
  • getExtent() is the bounding box of the archive in the CRS of the matrix set. For PMTiles it is in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857).

PMTilesVectorTileStore implements this on top of a PMTilesReader. It validates the archive's tileType at construction and throws UnsupportedTileTypeException if the archive is a raster archive.

docs.title: RasterTileStore
docs.text:
public abstract class RasterTileStore extends AbstractTileStore<RenderedImage> {
    public abstract String mimeType();
    public abstract BoundingBox2D getExtent();
}
  • mimeType() returns the on-disk MIME type of the encoded tiles (image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp, image/avif). Useful for HTTP Content-Type headers when proxying raw bytes, or for selecting an ImageWriter when re-encoding.
  • The payload type is the RenderedImage interface (not the concrete BufferedImage that ImageIO.read produces). The result flows directly into APIs like GridCoverageFactory.create(String, RenderedImage, ReferencedEnvelope) without intermediate copies.

PMTilesRasterTileStore implements this on top of a PMTilesReader. It decodes each tile by passing ImageIO.read as the mapper of PMTilesReader.getTile(long, IOFunction<InputStream, D>). The tile bytes are read into a buffer borrowed from a pool. The PMTiles header does not record the tile size: the store reads the size of the first tile when it is created.

WebP decoding is enabled out of the box by a bundled ImageIO plugin (com.github.usefulness:webp-imageio) registered via the JDK ServiceLoader. PNG and JPEG decoders ship with the JDK. AVIF is not bundled; add a JDK ImageIO plugin for AVIF if you need it. Without one, the raster store refuses AVIF archives with UnsupportedTileTypeException.

docs.title: PMTilesVectorTileStore / PMTilesRasterTileStore
docs.text:
Both wrappers are constructed from an existing PMTilesReader. They borrow the reader; closing the wrapper is not required (no resources beyond the underlying reader), but closing the reader releases the storage handle.

try (PMTilesReader reader = PMTilesReader.open(uri)) {
    PMTilesVectorTileStore vectorStore = new PMTilesVectorTileStore(reader);
    // or
    PMTilesRasterTileStore rasterStore = new PMTilesRasterTileStore(reader);
}

If the archive type doesn't match the wrapper, the constructor throws UnsupportedTileTypeException. An MLT archive (TILETYPE_MLT) is accepted by neither wrapper.

Optional caching: both classes expose a fluent cacheManager(CacheManager) setter. It selects the io.tileverse.cache.CacheManager used by the reader's cache of decoded directories. On PMTilesVectorTileStore it also selects the cache of decoded tiles. Without the setter, both caches use CacheManager.getDefault(). PMTilesRasterTileStore does not cache decoded images.

docs.title: TileJSON v3 model
docs.text:
The io.tileverse.jackson.databind.tilejson.v3 package contains a Jackson-annotated record model of the TileJSON 3.0.0 specification:

Type Role TileJSON Top-level record. Required fields: tilejson, tiles, vector_layers. Optional: attribution, bounds, center, description, etc. VectorLayer Per-layer descriptor: id, fields, description, minZoom, maxZoom (JSON minzoom, maxzoom). Returned by VectorTileStore.getVectorLayersMetadata(). TilesetType Enum: OVERLAY or BASELAYER, serialized as the JSON-spec strings.

The records use Jackson annotations directly; no custom mapper is required. The package is consumed by VectorTileStore and is the format the PMTiles reader pulls per-layer metadata from when present in the archive's JSON metadata blob.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
tileverse-storage gives one Java API over local files, HTTP, Amazon S3 and S3-compatible services, Azure Blob Storage and Data Lake Storage, and Google Cloud Storage. A Storage covers a container: a directory, a bucket, or a prefix. It lists, reads, writes, deletes, copies and presigns the objects under it, and declares which of these operations its backend supports.

Format readers that need byte ranges of one file, such as PMTiles, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF or Parquet readers, get a RangeReader from Storage.openRangeReader(key). See Read byte ranges.

docs.title: Supported backends
docs.text:
URI scheme Backend Notes file:, no scheme Local filesystem Real directories, atomic rename http:, https: HTTP / HTTPS Read-only; range GET s3: AWS S3 General-purpose buckets and S3 Express One Zone (Directory Buckets) az: Azure Blob Storage Flat keyspace + virtual directories. az://<account>/<container>/<path> addresses https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<path> (DuckDB / fsspec convention). abfs:, abfss: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 Real directories + atomic rename when HNS is enabled gs: Google Cloud Storage Flat or Hierarchical Namespace; HNS auto-detected

The URI scheme alone selects the backend, and no request is sent to choose it. An http(s) URL opens the HTTP backend, the URL of an object in a cloud service included: a public object reads without credentials, and a private one is refused (401 or 403; Azure Blob answers 404 or 409). To reach a cloud backend through an http(s) URL, name the provider with storage.provider (s3, azure, azure-datalake or gcs), or use the native scheme.

S3-compatible services, such as MinIO, Ceph, Garage or Cloudflare R2, work through the S3 backend. See Use each backend.

docs.title: Open a Storage
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.storage.Storage;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageFactory;

// Same call works for any supported URI scheme.
try (Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(URI.create("s3://my-bucket/datasets/v3/"))) {
    // ... use the Storage ...
}

StorageFactory.open(URI) opens the backend of the URI scheme. The overloads taking Properties or a StorageConfig also open the provider named by storage.provider when one is set. With no credential parameter, the cloud backends use the default credential chain of their SDK; Authenticate lists the alternatives.

docs.title: What can you do with it?
docs.text:
import io.tileverse.storage.CopyOptions;
import io.tileverse.storage.DeleteResult;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageEntry;
import io.tileverse.storage.WriteOptions;
import io.tileverse.storage.RangeReader;
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

try (Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(URI.create("s3://my-bucket/datasets/v3/"))) {

    // Stat (HEAD)
    storage.stat("year=2024/file.parquet").ifPresent(entry -> {
        System.out.println("size=" + entry.size() + " etag=" + entry.etag().orElse("none"));
    });

    // List with a glob; "**" walks the descendants
    try (Stream<StorageEntry> entries = storage.list("year=2024/**/*.parquet")) {
        entries.filter(e -> e instanceof StorageEntry.File)
                .forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.key()));
    }

    // Write a small object atomically
    storage.put("notes/hello.txt", "hello".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

    // Conditional write (compare-and-set on creation)
    storage.put("locks/leader",
            "node-1".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
            WriteOptions.builder().ifNotExists(true).build());

    // Range read
    try (RangeReader reader = storage.openRangeReader("year=2024/file.parquet")) {
        ByteBuffer buf = reader.readRange(0, 4096);
        // ...
    }

    // Delete + bulk delete
    storage.delete("notes/hello.txt");
    DeleteResult result = storage.deleteAll(List.of("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt"));
    System.out.println("deleted=" + result.deleted() + " failed=" + result.failed());

    // Server-side copy + move
    storage.copy("src.bin", "dst.bin", CopyOptions.defaults());
    storage.move("dst.bin", "moved.bin"); // atomic on local FS / DataLake Gen2 HNS / GCS HNS

    // Presigned GET URL (where supported)
    if (storage.capabilities().presignedUrls()) {
        URI url = storage.presignGet("file.parquet", Duration.ofMinutes(15));
        // share `url` with a client that doesn't have credentials
    }
}

Use each backend describes the glob syntax of list.

docs.title: Resource lifecycle
docs.text:
• Close a Storage when you no longer need it, for example with try-with-resources. The Storage instances of one account share one SDK client, counted by references: closing one Storage leaves the others working.
  • Close the streams returned by list(...) and openOutputStream(...), and the ReadHandles returned by read(...).
  • Closing a RangeReader releases only that reader. The Storage stays open.
